claims.claim: Borski says the third novella is told out of order with the reader left to piece the case together from a fragmentary narrative.
claims.source: Robert Borski, review of The Fifth Head of Cerberus, Ultan's Library, 28 August 2001
claims.quote: told anachronically, with the reader left to piece everything together

claims.claim: Wolfe told Science Fiction Studies that he writes a minimum of three passes over everything, an original plus at least two rewrites.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, 'On Encompassing the Entire Universe', Science Fiction Studies #46, vol. 15 part 3, November 1988
claims.quote: an original and then at least two rewrites

claims.claim: Wolfe said some of his work goes through fifteen or more drafts.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: some of it goes 15 or even more drafts

claims.claim: Wolfe said he rewrote the opening pages of The Fifth Head of Cerberus at least eight or ten times.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: I completely rewrote those opening pages at least eight or ten times

claims.claim: Wolfe said the reason he rewrote that opening so many times was to establish the feeling of stagnation that governs what follows.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: the feeling of stagnation which affects a lot of

claims.claim: Wolfe said getting the language right matters most when he is trying to capture a specific atmosphere or cultural attitude in a story.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: trying to capture a specific atmosphere or cultural attitude in a story

claims.claim: Wolfe rejected the reading that his refracted narrative methods are meant to mystify readers.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: is not to mystify my readers

claims.claim: Wolfe said he drew a floor plan of the house in Free Live Free because he otherwise got tangled in physical questions about the building.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: I had to draw a floor plan of

claims.claim: Wolfe listed the kind of physical question the floor plan settled, such as whether the street was visible from a given window.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: Could you see the street from this window

claims.claim: Wolfe said he checks that a recurring character is the same person on page 300 as on page 10, and rewrites the earlier page when he prefers the later version.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: the same person on page 300 as he was on page 10

claims.claim: Wolfe told Science Fiction Studies that memory is all we have, the present being a knife's edge and the future not existing.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988

claims.claim: McCaffery credits The Fifth Head of Cerberus with sure control of a variety of imaginative narrative voices.
claims.source: Larry McCaffery, editorial headnote to 'On Encompassing the Entire Universe: An Interview with Gene Wolfe', Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: sure control of a variety of imaginative narrative voices

claims.claim: McCaffery characterises the exposition of The Fifth Head of Cerberus as prismatic.
claims.source: Larry McCaffery, editorial headnote, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988

claims.claim: Novelist Max Gladstone says Wolfe's readers build interpretations by connecting sentences hundreds of pages apart rather than from anything stated outright.
claims.source: Max Gladstone, 'The Wolfeman', The Third Place (Substack), 2022
claims.quote: building theories by rubbing together two sentences two hundred pages apart

claims.claim: Gladstone says Wolfe's narrators claim eidetic memory and perfect recall and honesty, and then lie or forget.
claims.source: Max Gladstone, 'The Wolfeman', The Third Place (Substack), 2022
claims.quote: They assert their eidetic memories and perfect recall and utter honesty
